During the day, sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere and collides with gas molecules that are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light. This causes a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering, in which shorter wavelengths—like blue and violet—are scattered far more strongly than longer ones. Although violet light scatters even more than blue, our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and some of it is absorbed in the upper atmosphere, so the scattered light we see across the sky appears predominantly blue.
